texts.preamble: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Kailash on 10 May, 2016
texts.facts: Accused JUDGMENT: 1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules. The accused Kailash is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Kailash Trading Company, from where the food article, that is, 'Arhar Dal' was lifted for sampling. 2. As per the complaint, on 05.05.2008, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Chander Bhan Boora and Food Assistant (FA) J. S. Bisht under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Yogesh Partap reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Kailash Trading Company at Shop No. 13, Pul Mithai, Library Road, Azad Market, Tokriwalan, Delhi-110006, where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored for sale for human consumption. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Dal Arhar from the vendor lying in open gunny bag (ready for sale) bearing no label declaration, to which he had agreed. The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules. Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc. The price of sample was paid to the vendor. The vendor also failed to Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Kailash on 10 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105164859/ 1 disclose the name of the supplier of such commodity. Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA. Vide report dated 21.05.2008, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it was coloured with synthetic colouring matter 'Tartrazine'. Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI. After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court by FI on 21.08.2008 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act as well as Rules 23 and 29 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act, and also violation of section 14A of the PFA Act as punishable under section 16(1C) of the Act. 3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 21.08.2008. The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI C.B. Boora. On the basis of his deposition, charge was framed against the accused on 04.02.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. At the trial, the witness already examined in pre-charge stage was recalled for further cross-examination in post-charge stage and additionally, the prosecution examined PW-2 Sh. Yogesh Partap (SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA J. S. Bisht in post-charge stage. 4. At the trial, PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 who were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings, deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 05.05.2008 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Dal Arhar (ready for sale), thoroughly mixing it using a clean and dry jhaba, separately sealing, packing and marking the samples, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses. They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW- 1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C. Vendor furnished his statement Ex. PW-1/D. On the next working day that is 06.05.2008, one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/ E and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-1/F. PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, further investigation was carried out by PW-1 who sent letter Ex. PW-1/H to the STO to ascertain constitution of his business concern. Thereafter, sanction Ex. PW-1/I was taken from the Director PFA and after completion of the investigation, complaint Ex. PW-1/J was filed in the court. After this, intimation letter Ex. PW-1/K with copy of PA report was sent to the accused through registered post vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/L which was received undelivered. Thereafter, a copy was served personally upon the accused. 5. These witnesses were duly cross- examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein PW-1 and PW-2 denied that the accused was not present at the spot or that the proceedings were conducted while sitting at their office. PW-3 deposed that the jhaba and bottles used were already clean and dry and therefore they were not made further clean and dry at the spot. He denied that jhaba, envelope or bottles were not clean and dry or that some yellow colour was sticking to them. Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Kailash on 10 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105164859/ 2 6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 15.10.2013 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence. He claimed that the proceedings were conducted in his absence and that he was called at the spot after an hour. He stated that no efforts were made to join public witnesses and that payment was made to his workers and not him. He questioned the correctness of PA report and stated that no adulteration was made by him. He accepted that he was served with a copy of intimation letter personally by the FI. He also alleged that he had requested the FI to place the bill of the food article on record but he refused on the ground that the Dal was in loose condition. He chose to lead evidence in defence. 7. The accused examined himself as DW-1 in defence. He deposed that on 05.05.2008, at about 02.00 PM, PFA team came to his shop and lifted sample of Dal Arhar from him. He testified that he had purchased the Dal from S. K. International, Grain Merchants and Commission Agents, 4093, Main Road, Naya Bazar, Delhi-110006 and that he had also shown the Bill thereof to the FI (PW-1 herein) which he did not accept on the ground that sample had been taken from an open gunny bag. He placed on record the Bill Mark-DA. During cross-examination, he could not tell if the bags purchased by hum were bearing any brand mark or not. He denied that he was not having any bill at the time of sampling or that the said bill had been procured later. 8. The accused also summoned one Sh. Brij Arora and examined him as DW-1 (sic: DW-2). He deposed that he was the proprietor of S. K. International, 4093, Main Road, Naya Bazar, Delhi-110006 and proved the bill Ex. DW-1/A (earlier Mark-DA). Though he could not identify who had signed the bill on his behalf, yet stated that commodity was sold to Kailash Raju, Peeli Kothi, Delhi. During cross-examination, he identified the accused to whom he used to sell food grains and pulses. He however stated that he never sold Dal Arhar containing Tartrazine colour.
texts.arguments: 9. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 21.05.2008. It is pointed out that the accused has failed to exercise his right under section 13(2) PFA Act and failed to get the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL). It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony. It is also submitted that the bill Ex. DW-1/A is not reliable as it could not establish that the dal sold through this bill was the same as was lifted from the spot, or even that Kailash Raju as mentioned on this bill is the accused Kailash in this case. 10. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses. Ld. Counsel has contended that percentage or extent of synthetic colour Tartrazine has not been mentioned in the report of the chemical expert and it might be possible that only traces of colour were present. Relying upon the judgement of Maya Ram v. State of Punjab [1987(II) PFA Cases 320], it is contended that paper chromatography test used by the PA for detecting food colours is not a sure test and thus, the report of PA becomes unreliable. It is further submitted that Tartrazine is not a harmful colouring matter as its use is permitted in many food articles. Ld. Counsel has submitted that tartrazine is a water soluble colour and when the dal arhar is washed Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Kailash on 10 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105164859/ 3 before cooking, the said colour gets washed away and no harm is caused to the consumer. It is also argued that the accused was not the manufacturer of the article but was only a retailer who had purchased the commodity from another seller, for which he should not be held liable. It is submitted that the accused has proved the bill vide which the dal was purchased from him and thus, he is entitled to get the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) PFA Act. It is finally contended that the laboratory in which the sample was analysed and the testing method were not notified under the Rules and therefore the prosecution is bad in law. Be that as it may, under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be. Under section 2(ia)(b), it has to be established that the food article contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof. Even the judgement of Maya Ram v. State of Punjab [1987(II) PFA Cases 320] would not help the accused. This test is internationally recognised and accepted method to detect presence of colours in food articles. 23. The judgement in Maya Ram v. State of Punjab (supra), State v. Subhash Chand [2012(2) JCC 1052] and Daulat Ram v. State of Punjab [1979(II) PFA Cases 202], as relied upon by the defence, are clearly distinguishable on facts of this case. These judgements would apply only in those cases where some synthetic food colour is permitted to be used in a food article (like sweets) and the court has to determine if the synthetic colour found in the sample was permitted or unpermitted. In such a position, the Hon'ble Court had observed that paper chromatography test would not be sufficient Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Kailash on 10 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105164859/ 6 to find if the colour detected was permissible or not. But these judgements would not apply to those cases where use of such colours is absolutely prohibited and not permitted for use to any extent. Where the court need not go into the question if the colour detected was permissible or not, but has only to determine if any such colour was detected (as all such colours are prohibited), these judgements would not apply. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone, if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies. Relying upon the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector [2010(2) PFA Cases 310], the Ld. Defence counsel has argued that the prosecution was bad in law and no prosecution could have been launched because Section 23, which empowered the Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Kailash on 10 May, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/105164859/ 8 The relevant portion of the judgement relied upon by the Ld. Defence counsel reads as: "34. The present case would be squarely covered by the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Prem Ballab v. State (Delhi Administration) [(1977) 1 SCC 173]. In Hans Raj v. State of Punjab [1980(II) PFA Cases 396], there was evidence that no independent public persons had been joined. But in this case, there is evidence that attempt had been made to join public persons but they refused. Evidence to this effect has remained consistent. The findings in State of Himachal Pradesh v. Kamlesh Chand [2002(2) FAC 315] and State of Orissa v. Rabindra Sahu [2006(1) FAC 200] would not be applicable as in this case, all witnesses in this case have deposed about compliance of rules and there is nothing to conclude to the contrary. In Delhi Administration v. Rattan Lal [Crl. L. P. No. 42/2014, Delhi High Court, dated 30.07.2014] and Food Inspector v. Zahid [2014(2) FAC 524], there was evidence to show that jhaba was not made dry and clean.
